arXiv:2609.22618v1 [cond-mat.str-el] 18 Sep 2026

Probing dd-wave pairing in the tt-t′t^{\prime}-UU Hubbard model with tensor-backflow wave functions

Xiao Liang Email: xliang06@wm.edu Affiliation: Research Computing(Information Technology), William & Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia 23185, USA Affiliation: Department of Physics, William & Mary, Williamsburg, Virginia 23185, USA
Abstract

Building on the recently developed tensor-backflow method, which accurately describes energies and stripe states in the Fermi-Hubbard model, we investigate dd-wave pairing in the two-dimensional tt-t′t^{\prime}-UU Hubbard model. For the 8×88\times 8 lattice, we improve the wave function using symmetry projections followed by one Lanczos step, whereas for the 12×1212\times 12 and 16×1616\times 16 lattices, we apply one Lanczos step without symmetry projection. We focus primarily on the parameter regime with filling n=0.875n=0.875, on-site repulsion U=8U=8 and next-nearest-neighbor hopping t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t, a regime in which enhanced dd-wave pairing has been reported. The resulting energies are competitive with those obtained using state-of-the-art neural quantum states. For example, on a 16×1616\times 16 lattice with periodic boundary conditions, the tensor-backflow wave function after one Lanczos step without explicit symmetry enforcement achieves a relative energy difference of 4.4×10−34.4\times 10^{-3} from the symmetry-preserving neural quantum state result. From the real space pair correlations, for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t, we observe stronger dd-wave pair correlations together with the characteristic relative sign between horizontal and vertical bond-pair components. Compared with t′=0t^{\prime}=0, finite negative t′t^{\prime} increases the spectral weight of the corresponding pair-density matrix, which indicates the enhanced overall dd-wave pair fluctuations. The leading eigenvalue is enhanced on the 8×88\times 8 lattice for both with and without symmetry projections. For larger lattices such as 12×1212\times 12 and 16×1616\times 16, the leading pair-density matrix spectral weight is distributed among several nearly degenerate eigenmodes rather than being concentrated in a single dominant mode. This indicates enhanced and more broadly distributed dd-wave pair fluctuations, but no single eigenvalue exhibits the extensive scaling required for ODLRO.

I Introduction

The Fermi-Hubbard model is a paradigmatic model for studying the microscopic origin of unconventional superconductivity [1, 2]. Determining its ground state is challenging because several competing phases can be extremely close in energy [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. On finite lattices, the ground state can also depend sensitively on system size and boundary conditions. Therefore, to reduce the finite-size effect, the lattice size should be sufficiently large. The tt-t′t^{\prime}-UU Hubbard model is more challenging than the pure Hubbard model. The next-nearest-neighbor hopping t′t^{\prime} changes the Fermi surface and makes the ground state more sensitive to finite-size effects. Meanwhile, several nearly degenerate phases compete near the ground state.

Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) provides a flexible framework for approximating many-body ground states and their energies. Unlike many projector quantum Monte Carlo approaches, VMC does not suffer from a fermionic sign problem in sampling the probability distribution of a prescribed variational wave function [11, 12]; its accuracy instead depends on the expressiveness and optimization of the ansatz. Neural quantum states (NQSs) provide a powerful class of variational wave functions. Neural-network wave functions have achieved high accuracy for a variety of strongly correlated systems, including many-electron problems in continuous space [13, 14, 15, 16].

For lattice models, an effective variational wave function must combine sufficient expressive power with tractable optimization. In VMC, the variational parameters are typically optimized using gradient-based methods to minimize the energy expectation value. However, the effectiveness of VMC depends crucially on the quality of the variational wave function. Incorporating prior physical information, such as known sign structures or Hamiltonian symmetries, can substantially improve optimization and variational accuracy. The frustrated J​1J1-J​2J2 model provides one example. Near the maximal frustration J​2=0.5​J​1J2=0.5J1, employing a prior Marshall sign rule [17] significantly reduces the optimization difficulty [18, 19, 20]. In addition to incorporating prior sign structure, enforcing Hamiltonian symmetries can reduce the optimization difficulty and improve variational accuracy[21]. This strategy has also proved effective for the Fermi-Hubbard model [22, 23, 24].

Recently, the tensor-backflow wave function has shown high efficiency and accuracy in solving the Hubbard model [25]. For example, combined with one Lanczos step, the tensor-backflow wave function achieves energies competitive with Transformer-based NQS calculations [26], meanwhile the method has obtained charge-density-wave (CDW) and spin-density-wave (SDW) with periods of 1/n1/n and 2/n2/n, on the 16×1616\times 16 lattice with periodic boundary conditions (PBC), where nn is the electron filling. As a variational wave function, the tensor-backflow is optimized by first-order-gradient method with sufficient MC sample number, and it has sufficient expressive power for a wide range of parameters in the Fermi-Hubbard model. For example, for the case of n=0.875n=0.875, U=8U=8, t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t on the 12×1212\times 12 under PBC, the tensor-backflow has successfully obtained the width-4 stripe with the energy lower than the Transformer NQS.

In this work, we apply the tensor-backflow method on cases of n=0.875n=0.875, U=8U=8, t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t on square lattices up to the size 16×1616\times 16 under PBC and open boundary conditions (OBC). For the 8×88\times 8 case, we perform symmetry projections on the tensor-backflow wave function, followed by a Lanczos step. The best energy achieved in this work is -0.7441, which is 8.1×10−48.1\times 10^{-4} and 8.7×10−38.7\times 10^{-3} higher than those achieved by the Transformer NQS: -0.7447 [26], and the fully symmetrized Pfaffian: -0.7506 [23], respectively. For cases of 12×1212\times 12 and 16×1616\times 16, a Lanczos step is applied on the wave function. For the case of 16×1616\times 16 under PBC, we compare energies from different setups of pinning fields, and we find that the width-4 stripe gives the lowest energy. The best energy achieved in this work for the 16×1616\times 16 lattice is -0.7408, this is 6.5×10−36.5\times 10^{-3} lower than the Neural Pfaffian [22] and the relative energy differences with respect to state-of-the-art NQS results [24, 27] are below 4.5×10−34.5\times 10^{-3}. Furthermore, we calculate pair correlations and investigate components of the pair correlation, for both t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t and t′=0t^{\prime}=0 on all lattice sizes. For t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t, we find stronger dd-wave pair correlations than for t′=0t^{\prime}=0, together with the characteristic relative sign between horizontal and vertical bond-pair components, such benefit of t′t^{\prime} is also demonstrated by comparing eigenvalues of pair-density matrices. For the same lattice size, eigenvalues of t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t is generally higher than the counterparts of t′=0t^{\prime}=0. However, the largest eigenvalue of t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t is not higher than that of t′=0t^{\prime}=0 for lattices of 12×1212\times 12 and 16×1616\times 16.

II Tensor-Backflow method

We briefly review the tensor-backflow method introduced previously [25, 28]. The tensor-backflow wave function is constructed based on backflow corrections. In backflow corrections, the particle position is transformed as [29]:

𝐫αB=𝐫α+∑βηα​β​[𝐒]​(𝐫β−𝐫α),\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}^{B}=\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}+\sum_{\beta}\eta_{\alpha\beta}[\mathbf{S}](\mathbf{r}_{\beta}-\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}), (1)

where 𝐫α\mathbf{r}_{\alpha} are actual particle positions and ηα​β​[𝐒]\eta_{\alpha\beta}[\mathbf{S}] are variational parameters depending on the many-body state |𝐒⟩|\mathbf{S}\rangle. Consequently, the backflow-corrected orbital of a particle on 𝐫α\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}: ϕkB​(𝐫α)\phi_{k}^{B}(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}) is a linear combination of orbitals from backflow sites 𝐫δ\mathbf{r}_{\delta} [29, 30]:

ϕkB​(𝐫α)=∑𝐫δηα​δ​[𝐒]​ϕk​(𝐫δ),\phi_{k}^{B}(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha})=\sum_{\mathbf{r}_{\delta}}\eta_{\alpha\delta}[\mathbf{S}]\phi_{k}(\mathbf{r}_{\delta}), (2)

where 𝐫δ\mathbf{r}_{\delta} denote the sites considered in backflow corrections. For example, for nearest-neighbor (NN) backflow, 𝐫δ\mathbf{r}_{\delta} contains 𝐫α\mathbf{r}_{\alpha} and the NN sites. For all-site backflow, 𝐫δ\mathbf{r}_{\delta} covers all lattice sites. In original backflow corrections, for simplicity, η\eta depends on 𝐬⁡(𝐫α)\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}) and 𝐬⁡(𝐫δ)\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r}_{\delta}) instead of the full many-body state |𝐒⟩|\mathbf{S}\rangle [29, 30].

A full-rank tensor can represent an arbitrary function of several independent variables. For the function of ηα​δ​ϕk\eta_{\alpha\delta}\phi_{k} in the backflow correction, the independent variables are the particle position 𝐫α\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}, orbital index kk, configurations of 𝐬⁡(𝐫α)\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}) and 𝐬⁡(𝐫δ)\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r}_{\delta}). A tensor built on these variables has the representation ability beyond the product of ηα​δ\eta_{\alpha\delta} and ϕk\phi_{k}. To further improve the representation ability on backflow corrections, we consider the summation index of backflow terms as an additional independent degree of freedom. Thus, the single tensor is built as: g𝐫α,k,δ,𝐬⁡(𝐫α),𝐬⁡(𝐫δ)g_{\mathbf{r}_{\alpha},k,\delta,\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r}_{\alpha}),\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r}_{\delta})} [25]. The resulting wave function is represented by the Slater determinant:

w⁡(𝐒)=det​MB,w(\mathbf{S})=\mathrm{det}M^{B}, (3)

where the matrix element is built according to the backflow summation: Mi,kB=∑jg𝐫i,k,j,𝐬⁡(𝐫i),𝐬⁡(𝐫j)M_{i,k}^{B}=\sum_{j}g_{\mathbf{r}_{i},k,j,\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r}_{i}),\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r}_{j})}, where ii and jj are used for labeling particles and backflow terms, respectively.

A single full-rank tensor contains a number of variational parameters equal to the product of its dimensions. For a particular particle filling nn, the parameter number of gg scales quadratically and cubically with lattice size for a finite range backflow and all-site backflow, respectively. However, only a subset of these parameters contributes to a given amplitude w⁡(𝐒)w(\mathbf{S}). The computational complexity for generating one w⁡(𝐒)w(\mathbf{S}) is 𝒪⁡(Q​N3)\mathcal{O}(QN^{3}), where QQ is the number of backflow terms considered and NN is the particle number. For a lattice with MM sites, there are QQ=5, 9 and MM for NN, next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) and all-site backflow, respectively.

In the conventional Hartree-Fock construction in Eq.(2), the particle and orbital spin labels must match, resulting in a block-diagonal structure of MBM^{B} in spin space. This restriction can limit the expressive power for systems with nontrivial spin correlations. As the tensor representation is beyond the original backflow correction built from Hartree-Fock orbitals, all matrix elements in Mi,kBM_{i,k}^{B} are considered regardless of spins of orbital kk and particle ii.

A Hartree-Fock orbital without spin can be represented by a tensor containing dimensions of 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i} and kk. Without restricting the spin identity between the orbital and the particle, the unrestricted-Hartree-Fock (UHF) is represented by a tensor with the dimension of g𝐫i,k,σiUHFg_{\mathbf{r}_{i},k,\sigma_{i}}^{\mathrm{UHF}}, where σi\sigma_{i} denotes the particle spin. By expanding the UHF’s tensor, the remaining dimensions in the tensor-backflow are added as: g𝐫i,k,σi,2,j,𝐬⁡(𝐫j)g_{\mathbf{r}_{i},k,\sigma_{i},2,j,\mathbf{s}(\mathbf{r}_{j})}, where the dimension of 2 is for distinguishing double occupation on 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i}. Because the optimization cost of a UHF is low, the tensor-backflow wave function is initialized by a UHF to reduce the optimization cost.

The tensor representation is optimized by first-order gradient descent method, a parameter in the tensor is updated as [25, 31, 32]:

xt+Δ​t=xt−sgn⁡(Gx)​dx,x_{t+\Delta t}=x_{t}-\mathrm{sgn}(G_{x})d_{x}, (4)

where GxG_{x} is the gradient of parameter xx, dxd_{x} is the step size. The energy and gradients are estimated by Markov-Chain-Monte-Carlo process:

Gx=2​⟨E⁡(𝐒)​Ox​(𝐒)⟩−2​⟨E⁡(𝐒)⟩​⟨Ox​(𝐒)⟩,G_{x}=2\langle E(\mathbf{S})O_{x}(\mathbf{S})\rangle-2\langle E(\mathbf{S})\rangle\langle O_{x}(\mathbf{S})\rangle, (5)

where local estimators under a configuration |𝐒⟩|\mathbf{S}\rangle are: E⁡(𝐒)=∑𝐒′w⁡(𝐒′)/w⁡(𝐒)​⟨𝐒′​H^​𝐒⟩E(\mathbf{S})=\sum_{\mathbf{S}^{\prime}}w(\mathbf{S}^{\prime})/w(\mathbf{S})\langle\mathbf{S}^{\prime}\hat{H}\mathbf{S}\rangle and Ox​(𝐒)=∂ln​|w⁡(𝐒)|/∂xO_{x}(\mathbf{S})=\partial\mathrm{ln}|w(\mathbf{S})|/\partial x.

To improve the energy accuracy of tensor-backflow, subsequent methods such as symmetry projections and a Lanczos step are applied on the wave function. The wave function for symmetry projections is constructed as [22, 23]:

wsym​(𝐒)=∑T^∈GλG​ξ​(T^,𝐒)​w​(T^​𝐒),w^{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathbf{S})=\sum_{\hat{T}\in G}\lambda_{G}\xi(\hat{T},\mathbf{S})w(\hat{T}\mathbf{S}), (6)

where T^\hat{T} applies a symmetry operation on |𝐒⟩|\mathbf{S}\rangle, ξ⁡(T^,𝐒)\xi(\hat{T},\mathbf{S}) is the permutation sign from the symmetry operation and λG\lambda_{G} is the character of the symmetry representation. Another method to improve the wave function is a Lanczos step. It improves the wave function by constructing a state in Krylov subspace [33]:

|Ψp+1⟩=A⁡|Ψp⟩+B⁡|Ψp⟂⟩,|\Psi_{p+1}\rangle=A|\Psi_{p}\rangle+B|\Psi_{p}^{\perp}\rangle, (7)

where |Ψp⟂⟩=(H^−E)/σ⁡|Ψp⟩|\Psi_{p}^{\perp}\rangle=(\hat{H}-E)/\sigma|\Psi_{p}\rangle, with σ2\sigma^{2} the energy variance of |Ψp⟩|\Psi_{p}\rangle.

Both symmetry projections and a Lanczos step lead to multiple Slater determinants in the final wave function. However, even with the correct kinds of symmetries, symmetry projection can improve energy accuracy when the wave function isn’t trapped at local minima. Meanwhile, a Lanczos step preserves the wave function’s symmetry and it can improve the energy accuracy systematically [19, 25].

III Numerical Results

The Hamiltonian of the tt-t′t^{\prime}-UU Hubbard model is:

H^=−t∑⟨i​j⟩,σ(c^i​σ†c^j​σ+H.c.)−t′∑⟨⟨i​j⟩⟩,σ(c^i​σ†c^j​σ+H.c.)+U∑in^i↑n^i↓,\begin{split}\hat{H}=&-t\sum_{\langle ij\rangle,\sigma}(\hat{c}_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{H.c.})-t^{\prime}\sum_{\langle\langle ij\rangle\rangle,\sigma}(\hat{c}_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{j\sigma}+\mathrm{H.c.})\\ &+U\sum_{i}\hat{n}_{i\uparrow}\hat{n}_{i\downarrow},\end{split} (8)

where tt and t′t^{\prime} are strengths for NN and NNN hoppings, respectively. UU is the strength of on-site interactions, c^i​σ†​(c^i​σ)\hat{c}_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}(\hat{c}_{i\sigma}) creates (destroys) a particle of spin σ\sigma on the ii-th site, and the particle number operator n^i​σ=c^i​σ†​c^i​σ\hat{n}_{i\sigma}=\hat{c}_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}\hat{c}_{i\sigma}. We set t=1t=1 through our investigations.

To benchmark the tensor-backflow wave function, we first compare its pair correlations with exact results for the case of N↑=N↓=5N_{\uparrow}=N_{\downarrow}=5 on the 4×44\times 4 lattice with PBC [34]. The pair correlation is:

⟨Δd​(d)​Δd†​(0)⟩,\langle\Delta_{d}(d)\Delta_{d}^{{\dagger}}(0)\rangle, (9)

with Δd​(d)=cd,↑​∑δf⁡(δ)​cd+δ,↓\Delta_{d}(d)=c_{d,\uparrow}\sum_{\delta}f(\delta)c_{d+\delta,\downarrow}, where the dd-wave bond-sign structure f⁡(±ex)=−f⁡(±ey)=1f(\pm e_{x})=-f(\pm e_{y})=1. Pair correlation comparisons are depicted in Tab.(1). In the table, each result of tensor-backflow is obtained by the p=1p=1 wave function with 1×1071\times 10^{7} MC sample number. For each pair separation 𝐝=(dx,dy)\mathbf{d}=(\mathrm{dx},\mathrm{dy}), the tensor-backflow result agrees with the exact value. Based on Eq.(7), the number of determinants scales as 𝒪⁡(N)\mathcal{O}(N) in a wave function coefficient wp=1​(𝐒)w_{p=1}(\mathbf{S}). Because the configuration in each determinant is locally changed relative to the original one, only a few matrix elements are changed, thus the efficiency for generating one wp=1​(𝐒)w_{p=1}(\mathbf{S}) is significantly improved by reusing matrix elements. Because of the high efficiency, the MC sample number for each estimation is as large as 1×1071\times 10^{7}, meanwhile the estimation error of Eq.(9) is below 1×10−31\times 10^{-3}. Fig.(1) demonstrates the estimation convergence for the separation of (2,1)(2,1) and U=4U=4.

III.1 8×88\times 8 case

We first present results for dd-wave pair correlations at n=0.875n=0.875, U=8U=8 and t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t on the 8×88\times 8 lattice with PBC. The tensor-backflow wave function includes NNN backflow corrections. The tensor-backflow wave function contains 516096 variational parameters, based on the product of tensor dimensions. The tensor-backflow wave function is initialized from the noninteracting (UU​H​F=0U_{UHF}=0) UHF state.

In this work, we apply several post-optimization improvements to achieve high energy accuracy, we apply projections of half-sized translational symmetry TT and C4 rotational symmetry RR on the wave function, along with a Lanczos step. Tab.(2) depicts energy comparisons of various posterior optimizations. From the table, the original tensor-backflow achieves energies of -0.7374 and -0.7424, without and with a Lanczos step, respectively. The symmetry projection of either TT or RR improves the energy accuracy, and the energy after a Lanczos step is near -0.743. Energies are similar for RR projections with λG=±1\lambda_{G}=\pm 1, here we use the RR projection with λG=1\lambda_{G}=1. The best energy -0.7441 is achieved with symmetry projections of both TT and RR along with a Lanczos step. Compared with the Transformer NQS energy of -0.7447 [26] and the fully symmetrized Pfaffian energy of -0.7506 [23], our best energy: -0.7441, is higher by 8.1×10−48.1\times 10^{-4} and 8.7×10−38.7\times 10^{-3}, respectively.

Fig.(2) demonstrates the energy extrapolation for the 8×88\times 8 case. In the figure, TT and RR denote symmetry projections of the half-size translational invariance and the C4 rotational invariance, respectively. For both with and without a Lanczos step, energies achieved with symmetry projections are lower than those without symmetry projections. The energy extrapolation is just a demonstration of the method, and the extrapolated energy at zero variance is estimated as: -0.7455.

Fig.(3) depicts ground state patterns of wave functions with different posterior optimizations. All results in the figure are obtained by p=1p=1 wave functions. The ground state pattern of the tensor-backflow without any symmetry projection is depicted in Fig.(3)(a)(b), with width-4 stripes obtained successfully. A half-size translational symmetry projection TT reduces the spin density meanwhile preserves the charge density, depicted in Fig.(3)(c)(d). The symmetry projection of both half-size translational invariance TT and C4 rotational invariance RR reduces the spin density to nearly uniform meanwhile significantly reduces the charge density, depicted in Fig.(3)(e)(f). The results of both energy accuracy and ground state patterns demonstrate that symmetry projections can improve the tensor-backflow wave function on the 8×88\times 8 lattice, meanwhile a Lanczos step can significantly improve the energy accuracy.

Spin structure factors S⁡(kx=π,ky)S(k_{x}=\pi,k_{y}) for various kinds of wave functions are depicted in Fig.(11)(a), with the definition: S⁡(𝐤)=1M2​∑i​jei​𝐤⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j)​siz​sjzS(\mathbf{k})=\frac{1}{M^{2}}\sum_{ij}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})}s_{i}^{z}s_{j}^{z}, where sizs_{i}^{z} is defined in Fig.(3). From the figure, spin structure factors peaks at ky=3​π/4k_{y}=3\pi/4, indicating the width-4 stripe order. Meanwhile, symmetry projections redistribute the spectral weights thus moderately reduce the peaks.

Based on ground state results, we investigate dd-wave pair correlations of wave functions with different posterior optimizations on the 8×88\times 8 lattice with PBC. As depicted in Fig.(3)(a)(b), the tensor-backflow wave function produces the width-4 stripes in the ground state pattern, thus it lacks translational and rotational invariances. We compare how projections of half-size translational invariance and C4 rotational invariance can affect the dd-wave pair correlations. The s/ds/d-wave pair-field operator on site 𝐫i\mathbf{r}_{i} is [22, 32]:

Δs,d​(𝐫i)=12​[Aex​(𝐫𝐢)±Aey​(𝐫𝐢)],\Delta_{s,d}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=\frac{1}{2}[A_{e_{x}}(\mathbf{r_{i}})\pm A_{e_{y}}(\mathbf{r_{i}})], (10)

where ex,ye_{x,y} is the unit vector along x/y-axis and Aδ​(𝐫i)=∑±c𝐫i,↑​c𝐫i±δ,↓−c𝐫i,↓​c𝐫i±δ,↑A_{\delta}(\mathbf{r}_{i})=\sum_{\pm}c_{\mathbf{r}_{i},\uparrow}c_{\mathbf{r}_{i}\pm\delta,\downarrow}-c_{\mathbf{r}_{i},\downarrow}c_{\mathbf{r}_{i}\pm\delta,\uparrow}. The s/ds/d-wave pair correlation is defined as [22, 32]:

Ps,d​(𝐫i,𝐫j)=⟨Δs,d†​(𝐫i)​Δs,d​(𝐫j)+Δs,d​(𝐫i)​Δs,d†​(𝐫j)⟩.P_{s,d}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{j})=\langle\Delta_{s,d}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{r}_{i})\Delta_{s,d}(\mathbf{r}_{j})+\Delta_{s,d}(\mathbf{r}_{i})\Delta_{s,d}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{r}_{j})\rangle. (11)

By definition, Eq.(11) can be expanded to eight terms in total, with four terms in the format of Aδ1†​Aδ2A_{\delta_{1}}^{\dagger}A_{\delta_{2}} and four terms in the format of Aδ1​Aδ2†A_{\delta_{1}}A_{\delta_{2}}^{\dagger}, where δ1=ex,ey\delta_{1}=e_{x},e_{y} and δ2=ex,ey\delta_{2}=e_{x},e_{y}. Pair correlations for parallel and perpendicular pairs are with δ1=δ2\delta_{1}=\delta_{2} and δ1≠δ2\delta_{1}\neq\delta_{2}, respectively.

In this work, we consider the translational invariant definition of the dd-wave pair correlation, where the correlation under a pair separation 𝐝\mathbf{d} is averaged on the whole lattice:

Pd​(𝐝)=1M​∑i∈MPd​(𝐫i,𝐫i+𝐝),P_{d}(\mathbf{d})=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i\in M}P_{d}(\mathbf{r}_{i},\mathbf{r}_{i}+\mathbf{d}), (12)

where 𝐝\mathbf{d} is the pair separation and MM is the total site number. To reveal the bond-sign structure of dd-wave pair correlation, we consider parallel and perpendicular pairs in the dd-wave pair correlation defined in Eq.(12):

C​1​(δ1,δ2,𝐝)=14​M​∑i∈MAδ1†​(𝐫i)​Aδ2​(𝐫i+𝐝),C​2​(δ1,δ2,𝐝)=14​M​∑i∈MAδ1​(𝐫i)​Aδ2†​(𝐫i+𝐝),\begin{split}&C1(\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\mathbf{d})=\frac{1}{4M}\sum_{i\in M}A_{\delta_{1}}^{{\dagger}}(\mathbf{r}_{i})A_{\delta_{2}}(\mathbf{r}_{i}+\mathbf{d}),\\ &C2(\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\mathbf{d})=\frac{1}{4M}\sum_{i\in M}A_{\delta_{1}}(\mathbf{r}_{i})A_{\delta_{2}}^{{\dagger}}(\mathbf{r}_{i}+\mathbf{d}),\end{split} (13)

and the eight components from K​1K1 to K​8K8 are defined:

K1/2=C1/2(ex,ex),K3/4=C1/2(ey,ey),K5/6=C1/2(ex,ey),K7/8=C1/2(ey,ex),\begin{split}&K1/2=C1/2(e_{x},e_{x}),\ K3/4=C1/2(e_{y},e_{y}),\\ &K5/6=C1/2(e_{x},e_{y}),\ K7/8=C1/2(e_{y},e_{x}),\end{split} (14)

where components of 1, 3, 5, 7 have the form of A†​AA^{\dagger}A and components of 2, 4, 6, 8 have the form of A​A†AA^{\dagger}. Bonds in components of 1, 2, 3, 4 are parallel to each other and those in components of 5, 6, 7, 8 are perpendicular to each other. The dd-wave pair correlation defined in Eq.(12) is obtainable through the eight components: ∑if⁡(i)​K​i\sum_{i}f(i)Ki, where f⁡(i)=±1f(i)=\pm 1 for the first four and the last four components, respectively.

On the 8×88\times 8 lattice, we compare components in the dd-wave pair correlation for various kinds of wave functions in Fig.(4). Each estimation in the figure is achieved with the MC sample number in the magnitude of 4.6×1054.6\times 10^{5}. In the figure, we consider tensor-backflow wave functions without and with a Lanczos step, half-size translational symmetry projection TT, C4 rotational symmetry projection RR and symmetry projections of both TT and RR. In the figure, all wave functions within symmetry projections are without a Lanczos step. dx\mathrm{dx} and dy\mathrm{dy} depict the pair separation in Eq.(12) and Eq.(13) are along the x-axis and y-axis, respectively.

dd-wave pair correlations for pair separations along dy\mathrm{dy} and dx\mathrm{dx} are depicted in Fig.(4)(a)(b). From the insets, based on both p=0p=0 and p=1p=1 wave functions, the tensor-backflow state exhibits a nonzero long-distance pair correlation along dy\mathrm{dy}, whereas the correlation decreases toward zero along dx\mathrm{dx}, reflecting the broken rotational symmetry of the stripe state in Fig.(3)(a)(b). dy\mathrm{dy} and dx\mathrm{dx} depict pair separations along directions perpendicular to and parallel to the stripe in Fig.(3), respectively. From the insets, the projection of half-size translational invariance doesn’t change the dd-wave pair correlations. Meanwhile, the C4 projection approximately halves the correlation along dy\mathrm{dy} and generates an equivalent correlation along dx\mathrm{dx}. Along both dy\mathrm{dy} and dx\mathrm{dx}, the projection of T+RT+R has similar results to the projection of RR.

Fig.(4)(c)(d)(e)(f) depict the eight components defined in Eq.(14), for various kinds of wave functions and pair separations on the 8×88\times 8 lattice. For the pair separation of dy=L/2\mathrm{dy}=L/2, where LL is the lattice side length, the dd-wave bond-sign structure is clearly shown in Fig.(4)(c). From the tensor-backflow wave function for both p=0p=0 and p=1p=1, because of the separation of L/2L/2 on PBC, the pair components satisfy the half-lattice translation relations: K​1=K​2K1=K2, K​3=K​4K3=K4, K​5=K​8K5=K8 and K​6=K​7K6=K7. Meanwhile, the dd-wave bond-sign structure is shown by K​1≈−K​5K1\approx-K5, K​2≈−K​6K2\approx-K6, etc. That is, horizontal and vertical bond components have opposite signs. For the pair separation of dy=L/2−1\mathrm{dy}=L/2-1 depicted in Fig.(4)(d), despite the lack of half-size translational invariance for pair components, nonzero dd-wave pair correlation is also obvious. Fig.(4)(e) depicts the pair separation of dx=L/2\mathrm{dx}=L/2. From both p=0p=0 and p=1p=1 tensor-backflow wave functions, all eight components are close to zero when dx=L/2\mathrm{dx}=L/2. Fig.(4)(f) depicts the pair separation of dx=L/2−1\mathrm{dx}=L/2-1. Local nonzero dd-wave pair correlation exists based on both p=0p=0 and p=1p=1 tensor-backflow wave function. Meanwhile the projection of RR symmetrizes the pair correlation along dx\mathrm{dx} and dy\mathrm{dy}. Note that within the RR projection, a component under the same separation length are different along dx\mathrm{dx} and dy\mathrm{dy}. For example, K​1K1 for dx=3\mathrm{dx}=3 corresponds to K​3K3 for dy=3\mathrm{dy}=3 after the C4 rotational symmetry.

III.2 12×1212\times 12, 16×1616\times 16 case

For the case of n=0.875n=0.875, U=8U=8, t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t on the 12×1212\times 12 lattice with PBC. The tensor-backflow wave function used in this work was optimized in the previous literature [25]. The wave function was initialized with UU​H​F=4U_{UHF}=4, and the converged energies were -0.7370(3) for p=0p=0 and -0.7419(2) for p=1p=1. In contrast to the symmetry-preserving NQS result -0.7443 [27], the relative energy difference of p=1p=1 is 3.2×10−33.2\times 10^{-3}. On the 12×1212\times 12 lattice, energies of t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t are -0.7369(5) and -0.7370(5) after the RR projection with λG=±1\lambda_{G}=\pm 1, respectively. Furthermore, for the 12×1212\times 12 lattice, the weight of a 90-degree rotated configuration |wp=1​(T^​𝐒)||w_{p=1}(\hat{T}\mathbf{S})| is much smaller than the original one |wp=1​(𝐒)||w_{p=1}(\mathbf{S})|, thus configurations around |T^​𝐒⟩|\hat{T}\mathbf{S}\rangle are neglected when the MC sampling starts from configurations near |𝐒⟩|\mathbf{S}\rangle. Spin structure factors S⁡(kx=π,ky)S(k_{x}=\pi,k_{y}) for the 12×1212\times 12 lattice are depicted in Fig.(11)(b). Because of the side length 12, S⁡(𝐤)S(\mathbf{k}) doesn’t exactly peak at ky=3​π/4k_{y}=3\pi/4, however it peaks at nearest allowed momentums ky=2​π/3,5​π/6k_{y}=2\pi/3,5\pi/6.

We investigate the dd-wave pair correlations for cases of t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t and t′=0t^{\prime}=0 on the 12×1212\times 12 lattice under PBC within the symmetry broken but p=1p=1 wave functions. Fig.(5) depicts the pair correlations and components under various pair separations for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t and t′=0t^{\prime}=0. Each estimation in the figure is obtained by the p=1p=1 wave function within 4.6×1054.6\times 10^{5} MC samples. Here dx\mathrm{dx} and dy\mathrm{dy} denote pair separations along the x and y directions, respectively. In Fig.(5)(a), dd-wave pair correlations along dx\mathrm{dx} and dy\mathrm{dy} are different because of the symmetry broken state. For t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t, nonzero dd-wave pair correlation is generated along dx\mathrm{dx}. However, pair correlations for t′=0t^{\prime}=0 are close to zero along both dx\mathrm{dx} and dy\mathrm{dy}. This provides evidence that negative t′t^{\prime} enhances the dd-wave pair correlations. Fig.(5)(b) depicts the eight components defined in Eq.(14), for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t. From the figure, the nonzero pair correlation is accompanied by the expected dd-wave bond-sign structure at the largest pair separation along dx\mathrm{dx}. Meanwhile, the bond sign structrue varies at other pair separations. Along dy\mathrm{dy}, where zero pair correlation is expected from Fig.(5)(a), all components are close to zero.

We continue investigating cases of n=0.875n=0.875, U=8U=8, t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t on the 16×1616\times 16 lattice with PBC. Unlike the 8×88\times 8 and 12×1212\times 12 lattices, the tensor-backflow wave function requires additional pinning fields to guide the optimization. We find that the optimization is prone to becoming trapped in local minima even with various UU​H​FU_{UHF}. To achieve the best energy, we compare energies under various setups of pinning fields. The pinning fields are applied by:

H^P​F=H^+∑i∈P​Fhi​(ni↑−ni↓),\hat{H}_{PF}=\hat{H}+\sum_{i\in PF}h_{i}(n_{i}^{\uparrow}-n_{i}^{\downarrow}), (15)

where H^\hat{H} is the original Hamiltonian defined in Eq.(8) and hih_{i} defines the pinning fields. In this work we consider three kinds of pinning fields, denoted as PF1, PF2 and PF3. For PF1, hi=0.25×(−1)ixh_{i}=0.25\times(-1)^{i_{x}} for iy=2i_{y}=2 and hi=0.25×(−1)ix+1h_{i}=0.25\times(-1)^{i_{x}+1} for iy=14i_{y}=14. For PF2, hi=0.25×(−1)ixh_{i}=0.25\times(-1)^{i_{x}} for iy=2,10i_{y}=2,10 and hi=0.25×(−1)ix+1h_{i}=0.25\times(-1)^{i_{x}+1} for iy=6,14i_{y}=6,14. For PF3, hi=0.25×(−1)ixh_{i}=0.25\times(-1)^{i_{x}} for iy=1,9i_{y}=1,9 and hi=0.25×(−1)ix+1h_{i}=0.25\times(-1)^{i_{x}+1} for iy=5,13i_{y}=5,13. PF2 and PF3 differ only by a translation along dy\mathrm{dy}. After the UHF is optimized, the pinning fields are applied during the optimization steps, where the MC sample each step is 𝒪⁡(4.5×104)\mathcal{O}(4.5\times 10^{4}). After several thousands of optimization steps, the ground state pattern according to the pinning fields is established. Then, the pinning fields are removed and optimizations are continued with approximately 4.5×1054.5\times 10^{5} MC samples used at each optimization step.

Tab.(3) denotes how converged energies are sensitive to pinning fields, UU​H​FU_{UHF} and optimization step number. In the table, step number denotes optimization steps used for converging the energy after the pinning fields are removed. Energy convergences after removing the pinning fields are depicted in Fig.(6). From the Tab.(3) and Fig.(6), PF1 leads to the highest energy. Both PF2 and PF3 give similar energies after a similar step number, regardless of the UU​H​FU_{UHF}. Furthermore, the energy accuracy can be further improved by increasing the step number. As depicted in the figure, for the case of PF3 and UU​H​F=4U_{UHF}=4, increasing the step number from 1925 to 9013 further decreases the Ep=1E_{p=1} from -0.7401(2) to -0.7408(1), meanwhile, the energy of Ep=0=−0.7360​(7)E_{p=0}=-0.7360(7) corresponds to the Neural Pfaffians [22]. Therefore, the energy can be further lowered by continuing the optimization. This observation is consistent with the large numbers of optimization steps employed in recent NQS calculations [26, 27].

Fig.(7) depicts ground state patterns achieved under various kinds of pinning fields. Each spin density and charge density in the figure is obtained by p=1p=1 wave functions. In the figure, results PF1(a)(b) and PF2(c)(d) are obtained by the wave function within the step number about 2000. Meanwhile, the result of PF3(e)(f) is obtained by the wave function within the step number 9013. However, ground state patterns of the step number of 1925 and 9013 are similar for PF3. From the figure, even with the PF1, a width-4 stripe order is in the development. For PF2 and PF3, width-4 stripe order is successfully established. We also transfer the wave function converged under PF3 to OBC(g)(h), and the converged energy is Ep=1=−0.7097E_{p=1}=-0.7097. From the figure, width-4 stripe order is preserved in OBC, and the ground state is adjusted according to the boundary condition. Spin structure factors S⁡(kx=π,ky)S(k_{x}=\pi,k_{y}) for the 16×1616\times 16 lattice are depicted in Fig.(11)(c). From the figure, all cases of PF1, PF2, PF3 and OBC have the peak at ky=3​π/4k_{y}=3\pi/4, indicating the width-4 stripe order.

Fig.(8) depicts the dd-wave pair correlations and components for the 16×1616\times 16 lattice. In the figure, all results are obtained by p=1p=1 wave functions except the case of PF3 with TT projection. Comparisons between t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t and t′=0t^{\prime}=0 are depicted in Fig.(8)(a). From the figure, for the case of t′=0t^{\prime}=0, pair correlations decrease to zero in both dx\mathrm{dx} and dy\mathrm{dy}, thus we find no evidence for robust long-distance dd-wave pairing correlations at this lattice size. For the case of t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t, nonzero pair correlations exist under the largest pair separation along dx\mathrm{dx}. Components defined in Eq.(14) for dx=L/2\mathrm{dx}=L/2 are depicted in Fig.(8)(c)(d). From Fig.(8)(c), dd-wave bond-sign structure are generated for both PF1 and PF2. Although components of PF1 and PF2 have the opposite global sign. Fig.(8)(d) depicts results of PF3 and compares the components to the case of t′=0t^{\prime}=0. Because pinning fields of PF2 and PF3 differs only by a translation along dy\mathrm{dy}, dd-wave components from PF2 and PF3 are similar. For comparisons, components for t′=0t^{\prime}=0 are denoted in Fig.(8)(d) without errorbars for visibility. From the figure, all components of t′=0t^{\prime}=0 are close to zero, matching the zero dd-wave pair correlations in Fig.(8)(a).

The pair components in Eq.(14) are difficult to converge for the 16×1616\times 16 lattice, as they require a large MC number. Convergence of pair components are depicted in Fig.(12). In the figure, under the pair separation dx=L/2\mathrm{dx}=L/2, each estimation is obtained by the p=1p=1 wave-function, 829440 and 645120 MC samples are used for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t and t′=0t^{\prime}=0, respectively. From the figure, dd-wave bond-sign structure is revealed for the t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t case. However, for t′=0t^{\prime}=0, all components are close to zero.

We study the case of OBC to investigate dd-wave pair correlations under larger pair separations. To preserve the width-4 stripe order, the wave function is transferred from the case of PF3 under PBC, and it has been optimized for 1324 steps. The final converged energies are Ep=0=−0.7048​(7)E_{p=0}=-0.7048(7) and Ep=1=−0.7097​(1)E_{p=1}=-0.7097(1). For OBC, instead of averaging dd-wave pair correlations on the whole lattice denoted in Eq.(12), there are ix∈[3,14],iy=3i_{x}\in[3,14],i_{y}=3 for dy∈[3,11]\mathrm{dy}\in[3,11] and ix=3,iy∈[3,14]i_{x}=3,i_{y}\in[3,14] for dx∈[3,11]\mathrm{dx}\in[3,11]. From Fig.(7)(g)(h) and Fig.(11)(c), the width-4 stripe order is preserved under OBC. Fig.(8)(b) depicts dd-wave pair correlations for OBC. Different from PBC, pair correlations are close to zero under largest pair separations along both dx\mathrm{dx} and dy\mathrm{dy} for OBC.

III.3 Pair structure factor and pair-density matrix eigenvalues

Beyond the real-space bond-sign analysis, we investigate whether the tensor-backflow states exhibit off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO) [35] by examining the pair structure factor and the eigenvalue spectrum of the pair-density matrix on 8×88\times 8, 12×1212\times 12 and 16×1616\times 16 lattices.

To determine the type of the ground state, we calculate the pair structure factor [36]:

Sd​(𝐤)=1M2​∑i​jei​𝐤⋅(𝐫i−𝐫j)​⟨Δd†​(𝐫i)​Δd​(𝐫j)⟩,S_{d}(\mathbf{k})=\frac{1}{M^{2}}\sum_{ij}e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot(\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j})}\langle\Delta_{d}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{r}_{i})\Delta_{d}(\mathbf{r}_{j})\rangle, (16)

and eigenvalues of the pair-density matrix [37]:

Pi​j=⟨Δd†​(𝐫i)​Δd​(𝐫j)⟩,P_{ij}=\langle\Delta_{d}^{\dagger}(\mathbf{r}_{i})\Delta_{d}(\mathbf{r}_{j})\rangle, (17)

where Δd\Delta_{d} is defined in Eq.(10). We verify on 8×88\times 8 that the Lanczos step substantially improves the energy while leaving the pair correlations nearly unchanged. This motivates evaluating the computationally more demanding pair-density matrix using p=0p=0 wave functions on the larger lattices. To reduce the computational cost, we calculate the pair structure factor by p=0p=0 wave functions, each matrix element ⟨Δd†​Δd⟩\langle\Delta_{d}^{\dagger}\Delta_{d}\rangle is estimated using 115200 MC samples.

Fig.(9)(a)(b) depict pair structure factors for ky=0k_{y}=0 and kx=0k_{x}=0, respectively. From the figure, pair structure factors are centered at 𝐤=0\mathbf{k}=0 for all lattice sizes, indicating that the dominant pairing correlations occur at zero center-of-mass momentum. However, the peak does not visibly sharpen with increasing lattice size over the sizes studied, consistent with predominantly short-range pairing correlations.

Besides the pair structure factor, Fig.(10) depicts eigenvalues of pair-density matrices for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t and t′=0t^{\prime}=0 on 8×88\times 8, 12×1212\times 12 and 16×1616\times 16 lattices. From the figure, on the 8×88\times 8 lattice, the leading dd-wave pair-density matrix eigenvalue is enhanced for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t relative to t′=0t^{\prime}=0. For the 8×88\times 8 lattice, although symmetry projections improve the variational energy effectively, largest eigenvalues with and without symmetry projections are similar. For the 8×88\times 8 lattice, we evaluate the t′=0t^{\prime}=0 state using NN backflow (QQ=5) and NNN backflow (QQ=9) and the resulting spectra are similar, indicating that the enhanced pairing spectrum at t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t is not simply caused by the larger backflow range.

On larger lattices such as 12×1212\times 12 and 16×1616\times 16, the largest eigenvalue of t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t is not higher than that of t′=0t^{\prime}=0. However, near the largest eigenvalue of t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t, the dd-wave pair spectral weight is distributed among several nearly degenerate leading eigenmodes rather than being concentrated as strongly in a single dominant eigenmode, suggesting a larger number of nearly degenerate leading dd-wave pair modes for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t. Similar to the 8×88\times 8 case, the leading part of the pair-density matrix spectrum is generally shifted toward larger eigenvalues for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t, indicating stronger dd-wave pair correlations distributed among several modes.

In Fig.(10), each matrix element is estimated using 115200 MC samples. The resulting spectra show consistent qualitative trends among independently optimized wave functions. However, we do not use small differences between individual nearly degenerate eigenvalues as quantitative evidence. ODLRO requires the largest eigenvalue of the pair-density matrix to scale extensively, λm​a​x∝M\lambda_{max}\propto M in the thermodynamic limit [35, 37]. Based on Fig.(10), the leading eigenvalue does not show growth proportional to the system size over the lattice sizes studied. Based on Fig.(8)(b), the dd-wave pair correlation decreases to zero at large pair separations under OBC, thus the nonzero pair correlation under PBC should not be interpreted as robust ODLRO. Both Fig.(10) and Fig.(8)(b) suggest enhanced dd-wave pairing fluctuations rather than established superconducting ODLRO.

IV Discussions and conclusions

In this work, we apply the tensor-backflow wave function combined with various posterior optimization methods to investigate the dd-wave superconductivity in the tt-t′t^{\prime}-UU Hubbard model on square lattices. We compare cases of both t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t and t′=0t^{\prime}=0 on the same square lattice to investigate the effects of t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t.

We obtain energies competitive with current state-of-the-art NQS results. On the 8×88\times 8 lattice, we use symmetry projections along with a Lanczos step to improve the energy accuracy. The best energy achieved in this work for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t is -0.7441. The relative energy differences are 8.1×10−48.1\times 10^{-4} and 8.7×10−38.7\times 10^{-3} compared with Transformer NQS [26] and fully symmetrized Pfaffian [23], respectively. On the 12×1212\times 12 lattice, we use the tensor-backflow wave function optimized in the previous literature [25], within the energy Ep=1=−0.7419​(2)E_{p=1}=-0.7419(2), and the relative energy difference to the symmetry-preserving NQS result is 3.2×10−33.2\times 10^{-3}. On the 16×1616\times 16 lattice, we optimize the wave function using pinning fields. We compare states obtained with different pinning field protocols at comparable optimization stages. and find that the width-4 stripe order gives the lowest energy, and the relative energy difference is 4.4×10−34.4\times 10^{-3} relative to the symmetry-preserving NQS. Furthermore, we show that the energy accuracy can be improved by simply increasing optimization steps, however the qualitative stripe pattern remains unchanged.

In this work, although a Lanczos step substantially lowers the energy, comparison of the p=0p=0 and p=1p=1 states shows that the qualitative dd-wave pairing behavior is already captured by the original tensor-backflow state. This illustrates that, in a regime containing several nearly degenerate competing states, improvements in variational energy do not necessarily lead to equally large changes in order-sensitive observables. It is therefore important to compare both energies and order-sensitive observables across competing variational states.

We have compared real-space dd-wave pair correlations, pair structure factors, and pair-density matrix spectra for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t and t′=0t^{\prime}=0. On the 8×88\times 8 lattice, the leading pair-density matrix eigenvalue is enhanced for t′=−0.2​tt^{\prime}=-0.2t. On the 12×1212\times 12 and 16×1616\times 16 lattices, negative t′t^{\prime} enhances the leading portion of the pair-density matrix spectrum, with the spectral weight distributed among several nearly degenerate modes. Because the p=0p=0 wave function contains no explicit pairing determinant or pairing function, these enhanced dd-wave correlations arise from the configuration-dependent backflow structure of the variational state. Overall, negative t′t^{\prime} enhances dd-wave pairing fluctuations in the width-4 striped state, but neither the pair structure factor nor the finite-size scaling of the pair-density matrix spectrum establishes superconducting ODLRO up to 16×1616\times 16.
